parsed.headline: Minority caucus in Ghana calls for independent audit of GH¢49.72 million South Africa evacuation expenditure

pages.text: The New Patriotic Party (NPP) Minority caucus in Ghana has called for an independent audit of a GH¢49,721,786 evacuation exercise conducted in South Africa, alleging that documentation provided by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs leaves more than GH¢16.4 million requiring further explanation. Nana Asafo-Adjei Ayeh, the Bosome-Freho MP and Deputy Ranking Member of Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee, presented these allegations following a review of over 200 pages of documents released by Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa in response to a Right to Information (RTI) request. The Minority alleges the records contain discrepancies involving reintegration grants, transport allowances, commercial flight records, duplicate entries, and payments involving minors, arguing the documents do not fully reconcile with the reported expenditure and the total of 1,964 evacuees. These allegations do not establish that funds were stolen or that beneficiary numbers were deliberately inflated, but the Minority maintains that the emergency nature of the operation does not relieve the government of its obligation to account for the funds spent.

The evacuation exercise was undertaken following xenophobic violence and intimidation against foreign nationals in South Africa. According to the Ministry, the operation began on May 27 and concluded on September 4, 2026, when the final group of 41 returnees arrived in Ghana. On September 7, Minister Ablakwa announced the total expenditure of GH¢49,721,786, which comprised GH¢33,721,786 in direct government funding and GH¢16 million in support attributed to Engineers & Planners, a company owned by businessman Ibrahim Mahama. The reported costs covered chartered flights, commercial airline tickets, ground transportation, feeding, accommodation, medical care, reintegration support, and other logistical expenses. The government stated that each evacuee received a GH¢5,000 reintegration grant and a GH¢500 transport allowance.

parsed.headline: Cleveland-Cliffs CEO prepared to fight Canadian government in court over Stelco layoffs

pages.text: Lourenco Goncalves, CEO of the American company Cleveland-Cliffs, stated on Sunday that he is prepared to fight the Canadian government in court to preserve plans to lay off hundreds of workers at Hamilton-based steelmaker Stelco. Speaking on CBC's Rosemary Barton Live, Goncalves disputed claims by the Canadian government that the company is violating binding employment commitments made under the Investment Canada Act during its 2024 purchase of Stelco. Goncalves argued that there is no provision in the contract requiring the company to maintain specific employment levels every day throughout the five-year period through 2029. He stated, “If that was an imposition of the Canadian government, I would not have accepted.”

The dispute follows an ultimatum issued last week by Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, who demanded the company share a plan to save up to 500 jobs that could be impacted at the Hamilton plant or face potential legal action. Joly asserted that the purchase included undertakings to continue employing at least the same number of unionized employees and the vast majority of non-unionized employees as were employed when the transaction was announced. Prime Minister Mark Carney also stated last week that Ottawa would use all available powers to pursue the Ohio-based company to the “fullest extent of the law.”

Stelco Inc. responded to Joly in a letter, stating the company will proceed with the layoffs and calling the government's characterization of a breach of undertakings “false.” Goncalves reiterated the company's position that the layoffs are a temporary measure intended to last until Canada and the U.S. reach a trade agreement, at which point jobs would be restored. While Stelco has cited U.S. President Donald Trump's 50 per cent tariffs as a factor in its economic struggles, Goncalves voiced support for those tariffs and noted he is open to selling the company.

parsed.headline: Four placed on remand in Dhaka over alleged defacing of Tagore mural

pages.text: A Dhaka court on October 11, 2026, placed four individuals on remand following their alleged involvement in an attempt to deface a mural of Nobel laureate poet Rabindranath Tagore in Segunbagicha, Dhaka. According to The Daily Star Bangladesh, the individuals were detained on October 10, 2026, in connection with the incident occurring on a wall opposite the Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy.  The court, presided over by Dhaka Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Jashita Islam, ordered a three-day remand for Rashtra Sanglap Forum President ANM Ayas and Sakibul Hasan, and a two-day remand each for Sujon Mia and Marzia Khandaker Rimi. Additional Public Prosecutor Muhammad Shamsud Doha Sumon stated the order followed a 10-day remand prayer from police.  The case was filed at Shahbagh Police Station involving allegations of criminal conspiracy, inciting enmity between classes, and inciting religious hatred. Police reports allege that on October 9, Ayas announced intentions to erase the mural by whitewashing it. On October 10, the group reportedly went to the site, where Rimi allegedly smeared black ink over the mural of Tagore and attempted to incite religious hatred related to the upcoming Durga Puja. The mural was part of a series of portraits of 10 prominent cultural figures painted on a boundary wall after the Dhaka South City Corporation cleared the adjacent footpath of encroachments on October 5.
